name: C++
description: Object lifetime, RAII, move semantics, templates and the undefined behaviour that separates working code from lucky code.

modules.name: The Big Picture
modules.description: What C++ is, what it is for, and the words everything else builds on.

cards.prompt: What is C++, and what is it mainly used for?
cards.answer: A compiled, high-performance, multi-paradigm language that extends C with classes, templates and automatic resource management. It powers game engines (Unreal), web browsers (Chrome, Firefox), trading systems, databases, embedded and desktop software — anywhere speed and control matter.
cards.explanation: C++'s motto is "zero-cost abstractions": features such as classes and templates should cost nothing at run time compared with hand-written C. That makes it fast, but the language is large and has many sharp edges.

resources.title: Standard C++ — A tour of C++

cards.prompt: Who created C++, and how did it start?
cards.answer: Bjarne Stroustrup at Bell Labs, starting in 1979 as "C with Classes"; it was renamed C++ in 1983. It is now an ISO standard updated every three years (C++11, 14, 17, 20, 23).
cards.explanation: C++11 was such a large change that people speak of "modern C++" — code written with smart pointers, move semantics, `auto` and lambdas looks very different from 1990s C++. Learning resources older than C++11 teach habits that are now discouraged.

cards.prompt: How is a C++ program built and run?
cards.answer: A compiler (GCC's `g++`, Clang's `clang++` or Microsoft's MSVC) compiles each source file to machine code and the linker combines them into an executable. Larger projects describe the build with CMake.
cards.explanation: C++ compiles to native code, so the program runs with no virtual machine — but it must be rebuilt for each platform. Compile times can be long because headers are re-processed in every file that includes them; C++20 modules aim to fix that.

cards.prompt: What does a minimal C++ program look like?
cards.answer: `<iostream>` provides `std::cout`, the standard output stream; `<<` sends text to it. `std::` is the standard library's namespace.
cards.explanation: C++23 adds `std::println`, which is closer to Python's `print`, but `std::cout` is what most existing code uses. `main` returning without a `return` statement is allowed in C++ and means success (0).

cards.prompt: What kind of language is C++: typing, memory and paradigms?
cards.answer: Statically typed. Memory is managed by you, but idiomatically through RAII — objects release their resources (memory, files, locks) automatically in their destructor when they go out of scope, with smart pointers (`std::unique_ptr`, `std::shared_ptr`) instead of raw `new`/`delete`. It supports procedural, object-oriented and generic (template) programming.
cards.explanation: There is no garbage collector, so cleanup timing is deterministic — a key reason games and real-time systems use C++. The cost is that memory-safety bugs remain possible, just less likely with modern idioms.

cards.prompt: What is the C++ Standard Library (and the STL)?
cards.answer: The library every C++ compiler ships: containers (`std::vector`, `std::map`, `std::string`), algorithms (`std::sort`, `std::find`), smart pointers, I/O streams, threads and more. "STL" originally named the containers-and-algorithms part and is often used for the whole thing.
cards.explanation: Reach for standard containers before writing your own: `std::vector` should be your default sequence container. C++ has no single official package manager; projects use vcpkg or Conan, or vendor dependencies via CMake.

modules.name: Objects, Lifetime & RAII
modules.description: Construction, destruction, ownership and the rules that keep C++ memory-safe by design.

cards.prompt: What is RAII, and why does it matter more in C++ than almost anywhere else?
cards.answer: Resource Acquisition Is Initialisation: a resource is owned by an object, acquired in its constructor and released in its destructor. Because destructors run deterministically on scope exit — including during stack unwinding — cleanup is automatic and exception-safe.
cards.explanation: RAII is why `std::lock_guard`, `std::unique_ptr` and `std::fstream` need no `finally`. Every raw `new`, `malloc`, `fopen` or manual `lock` in modern C++ should be wrapped in a type whose destructor does the release.

cards.prompt: What is the Rule of Zero / Three / Five?
cards.answer: Rule of Zero: design classes that need no custom copy/move/destructor by holding RAII members. If you must write one of destructor, copy constructor or copy assignment, you probably need all three — plus the move constructor and move assignment, making five.
cards.explanation: The special members interact: declaring a destructor suppresses implicit move operations, silently degrading moves into copies. Prefer Rule of Zero — let `std::vector`, `std::string` and smart pointers own the resources and write none of the five.

cards.prompt: `std::unique_ptr` vs `std::shared_ptr`
cards.answer: unique_ptr is a single owner with zero overhead; shared_ptr is reference-counted with real costs.

left.title: unique_ptr
points: Same size as a raw pointer, no atomic traffic
Expresses ownership transfer in the signature

right.title: shared_ptr
points: Shared ownership via an atomic refcount
Two allocations unless you use make_shared
Cycles leak — break them with weak_ptr
Only when lifetime genuinely is shared

cards.explanation: Reach for `unique_ptr` first and upgrade only when several owners really can outlive each other. Passing `shared_ptr` everywhere hides ownership and adds atomic increments on every copy — a measurable cost in hot paths.

cards.prompt: What is undefined behaviour here?
cards.answer: `s` is destroyed when `greet` returns, so `r` binds to a dead object — a dangling reference. Return by value instead; copy elision makes it free.
cards.explanation: Binding a const reference to a temporary extends its lifetime, but returning a reference to a local never does. Return by value: guaranteed copy elision (C++17) constructs the result directly in the caller's storage.

cards.prompt: You delete a derived object through a base-class pointer. What must be true, and what happens if it is not?
cards.answer: The base destructor must be `virtual`. Otherwise the behaviour is undefined — typically only the base part is destroyed, leaking the derived members.
cards.explanation: A non-virtual destructor means the call is resolved statically to the base version. Rule of thumb: a class with any virtual function that is deleted polymorphically needs a virtual destructor; a base not meant for polymorphic deletion should have a protected non-virtual one.

cards.prompt: How is a virtual call typically implemented?
cards.answer: Each polymorphic class has a vtable of function pointers; each object stores a vptr to its class's vtable. A virtual call loads the vptr, indexes the vtable and calls through the pointer.
cards.explanation: That is two dependent loads plus an indirect branch — cheap, but not free, and usually unable to inline. It also explains why virtual calls in constructors resolve to the base version: the vptr is updated as each base sub-object is constructed.

modules.name: Move Semantics & Templates
modules.description: Value categories, perfect forwarding, templates and the standard library idioms built on them.

cards.prompt: What are lvalues, prvalues and xvalues?
cards.answer: An lvalue has identity and cannot be moved from implicitly. A prvalue is a pure temporary with no identity. An xvalue has identity but is expiring — safe to move from. Glvalue = lvalue + xvalue; rvalue = prvalue + xvalue.
cards.explanation: `std::move` does not move anything — it is a cast to an rvalue reference, producing an xvalue so overload resolution picks the move overload. `std::forward` conditionally casts, preserving the caller's value category in templates.

cards.prompt: What is the state of `a` after the move?
cards.answer: `a` is in a valid but unspecified state. You may assign to it or destroy it; you must not assume it is empty or read its value meaningfully.
cards.explanation: The standard library guarantees moved-from objects are valid but unspecified — most implementations leave `std::string` empty, and relying on that is non-portable. Assign a fresh value before use, or treat the variable as dead.

cards.prompt: Why can this crash?
cards.answer: `push_back` may reallocate, invalidating all references, pointers and iterators into the vector. `first` then dangles.
cards.explanation: Know each container's invalidation rules: vector invalidates everything on reallocation and on insert/erase before the position; `std::deque` invalidates iterators but not references on end insertion; node-based containers (list, map, unordered_map) keep references stable except for erased elements.

cards.prompt: Why do template definitions usually live in headers?
cards.answer: Templates are instantiated at the point of use, so the compiler needs the full definition in every translation unit that uses them. Otherwise you get link errors for the missing instantiation.
cards.explanation: The alternatives are explicit instantiation in one TU (fine when the set of types is known and small) or C++20 modules. This is also why heavy template use slows builds so dramatically: the same code is parsed and instantiated repeatedly.

cards.prompt: Name the classic sources of undefined behaviour in C++.
cards.answer: Reading uninitialised values, out-of-bounds access, use-after-free, dangling references, signed integer overflow, data races, null dereference, violating strict aliasing, and infinite loops with no side effects.
cards.explanation: UB is not 'it crashes' — the optimiser is entitled to assume it never happens, so it can delete your null check or your bounds test. Build with `-fsanitize=address,undefined` in CI; ASan and UBSan catch most of this list at the moment it happens.

cards.prompt: Complexity of `std::vector::push_back`?
cards.answer: Amortised O(1); an individual call is O(n) when it reallocates.

complexity.time: O(1) amortised, O(n) worst per call

cards.explanation: Growth is geometric (typically 1.5x or 2x), so n pushes cost O(n) total copies/moves. Call `reserve` when the final size is known: it removes the reallocation spikes and the iterator invalidation that comes with them.

cards.prompt: How should a function take a `std::string` parameter it intends to store?
cards.answer: Take it by value and `std::move` it into place — one copy for lvalue callers, zero for rvalue callers. Take `const&` only when you never store it.
cards.explanation: By-value-then-move collapses the two overloads (`const&` and `&&`) into one function with near-optimal cost. For a read-only parameter that is never stored, `const std::string&` or `std::string_view` avoids any copy at all.

modules.name: Language Core
modules.description: Pointers and references, const-correctness, construction, conversions, lambdas and compile-time programming.

cards.prompt: Pointer vs reference
cards.answer: A reference is an alias that must be bound at initialisation and can never be reseated or null; a pointer is an object holding an address that can be null, reassigned and do arithmetic.

left.title: Pointer `T*`
points: Can be null — must be checked
Can be reseated to point elsewhere

right.title: Reference `T&`
points: Used exactly like the object itself

cards.explanation: Guideline: use references for parameters that must refer to something, pointers (or `std::optional<T&>`-like wrappers, or smart pointers for ownership) when "nothing" is a valid value. A raw pointer in modern C++ should mean "non-owning, possibly null" — never ownership.

resources.title: C++ Core Guidelines — F.60: Prefer T* over T& when "no argument" is a valid option

cards.prompt: What is the difference between `const T*`, `T* const` and a `const` member function?
cards.answer: `const T*` (pointer to const): you cannot modify the pointee, but you can repoint it. `T* const` (const pointer): you cannot repoint it, but you can modify the pointee. A `const` member function (`int size() const`) promises not to modify the object and is the only kind callable on a const object.
cards.explanation: Read declarations right to left: `const char* const p` is "p is a const pointer to const char". Const-correctness spreads: mark every non-mutating member function `const` from day one, because retrofitting it later ripples through the whole codebase. `mutable` exempts caches and mutexes.

resources.title: C++ Core Guidelines — Con: Constants and immutability

cards.prompt: Why is `size_` garbage even though the initialiser list looks correct?
cards.answer: Members are initialised in their *declaration* order, not the order in the initialiser list. `buffer_` is declared first, so it is initialised using `size_` before `size_` has been set. Declare members in dependency order (and enable `-Wreorder`).
cards.explanation: Always use member initialiser lists rather than assignment in the constructor body — they initialise instead of default-constructing then assigning, and they are required for references, const members and types without default constructors. Default member initialisers (`int size_ = 0;`) cover the common case.

resources.title: cppreference — Constructors and member initializer lists

cards.prompt: Why does `send(42)` compile, and what is the fix?
cards.answer: A single-argument constructor doubles as an implicit conversion, so `42` silently becomes `Message(42)` — a message of 42 bytes, not the number 42. Mark single-argument constructors `explicit` unless implicit conversion is genuinely intended.
cards.explanation: Implicit conversions are how surprising overloads get selected and how units get mixed up. The Core Guidelines default is `explicit` for single-argument constructors and conversion operators; `std::string` from `const char*` is a deliberate exception.

resources.title: C++ Core Guidelines — C.46: By default, declare single-argument constructors explicit

cards.prompt: This loop is slow and its changes are lost. Why?
cards.answer: `auto` deduces a value type, so each element is copied — expensive for strings, and the `+=` modifies the copy. Use `auto&` to modify in place and `const auto&` to read without copying.
cards.explanation: Rule of thumb for range-for: `const auto&` by default, `auto&` to mutate, plain `auto` only for cheap types you mean to copy, and `auto&&` in generic code. The same copy trap applies to structured bindings: `for (auto [k, v] : map)` copies every pair.

cards.prompt: Why is this callback undefined behaviour when it eventually runs?
cards.answer: `[&]` captures `count` by reference, but `count` is a local that dies when `schedule` returns. The callback runs later and touches a dead stack slot. Capture by value (`[count]`), or move ownership in (`[p = std::move(ptr)]`).
cards.explanation: Reference captures are only safe when the lambda cannot outlive the scope — as with algorithms like `std::sort`. Anything stored, returned or run asynchronously should capture by value or own its data. Capturing `this` has the same danger when the object dies first.

cards.prompt: What are `std::optional`, `std::variant` and `std::expected` for?
cards.answer: `optional<T>` holds a T or nothing — a typed replacement for sentinel values and nullable pointers. `variant<A, B>` holds exactly one of several types, visited with `std::visit`. `expected<T, E>` (C++23) holds a value or an error, like Rust's `Result`.
cards.explanation: All three store their contents inline, with no heap allocation. They make "maybe absent" and "one of several" explicit in signatures instead of documented in comments. `variant` plus `std::visit` gives exhaustive handling of closed sets of alternatives.

cards.prompt: Why does this print garbage?
cards.answer: `std::string_view` does not own its characters. `make_name()` returns a temporary `std::string` that is destroyed at the end of the full expression, leaving `name` pointing into freed memory.
cards.explanation: Use `string_view` for parameters (read-only, no copy, accepts literals and strings alike), but never store one that may outlive its source, and never return one that refers to a local or temporary. `std::span` has exactly the same caveat for arrays.

cards.prompt: What do `constexpr`, `consteval` and `constinit` mean?
cards.answer: `constexpr` allows (but does not require) evaluation at compile time when inputs are constant. `consteval` requires compile-time evaluation. `constinit` guarantees a static variable is initialised at compile time, avoiding the static initialisation order fiasco.
cards.explanation: Compile-time evaluation catches errors early (UB in a constant expression is a compile error) and removes runtime cost for lookup tables and parsers. Most of the standard library — including `std::vector` and `std::string` in C++20 — is now usable in constexpr contexts.

cards.prompt: What problem do C++20 concepts solve?
cards.answer: They state template requirements explicitly — `template <std::integral T> T gcd(T a, T b)` or `requires std::sortable<It>` — so misuse fails at the call site with a readable error, instead of pages of errors from deep inside the template.
cards.explanation: Concepts replace SFINAE and `enable_if` tricks for constraining overloads. Prefer standard concepts (`std::ranges::range`, `std::invocable`, `std::totally_ordered`) and name your own after real semantic requirements, not syntax.

cards.prompt: `enum class` vs plain `enum`
cards.answer: Scoped enums (`enum class Color { Red }`) require qualification and never convert implicitly to integers; plain enums leak their names into the enclosing scope and convert to int silently.

right.title: enum
points: Names leak into the surrounding scope
Different enums compare with each other

cards.explanation: Use `enum class` by default. Plain enums let you compare a `Color` with a `Fruit` or pass one where an int is expected without complaint. Specify an underlying type (`enum class Op : std::uint8_t`) for serialisation and ABI stability.

modules.name: STL, Concurrency & Build
modules.description: Containers and algorithms, noexcept moves, threads and locks, the compilation model and CMake.

cards.prompt: Which standard container should be your default, and when do you pick `map`, `unordered_map` or `list`?
cards.answer: `std::vector` by default — contiguous, cache-friendly, fastest for almost everything. `std::unordered_map` for key lookup, `std::map` when you need sorted order or range queries, and `std::list` only when you need stable iterators across frequent middle insertions.
cards.explanation: Measure before leaving vector: a linear scan over a small vector often beats a map because of cache locality. `std::deque` for push/pop at both ends; `std::array` for fixed size; and flat maps (C++23 `std::flat_map`) for read-heavy lookups.

cards.prompt: Why prefer standard algorithms and ranges over hand-written loops?
cards.answer: They name the intent (`std::ranges::sort`, `find_if`, `any_of`, `transform`), are well tested and optimised, and are harder to get subtly wrong. C++20 ranges accept whole containers and compose lazily with views: `v | std::views::filter(pred) | std::views::transform(f)`.
cards.explanation: The classic trap is the erase-remove idiom: `std::remove` only moves elements; you must also `erase` — C++20 adds `std::erase_if(container, pred)` to do both. Views are lazy and non-owning, so a view over a temporary container dangles.

cards.prompt: Your type has a fast move constructor, yet `std::vector` copies every element when it grows. Why?
cards.answer: The move constructor is not `noexcept`. To keep its strong exception guarantee during reallocation, vector uses `std::move_if_noexcept` and falls back to copying when a move might throw. Mark move operations `noexcept`.
cards.explanation: Defaulted move operations are `noexcept` automatically when all members' moves are. This one keyword can change the complexity of growth from copying strings to swapping pointers. Destructors are implicitly `noexcept`; keep them that way.

cards.prompt: `push_back` vs `emplace_back`
cards.answer: `push_back` takes an already-constructed object (copying or moving it in); `emplace_back` forwards constructor arguments and builds the element in place.

left.title: push_back(x)
points: Takes a `T` — copies or moves it

right.title: emplace_back(args...)
points: Avoids a temporary for multi-arg types

cards.explanation: For an existing object or a temporary of the same type, the two are equivalent after moves. `emplace_back` can also call `explicit` constructors, which can hide mistakes: `v.emplace_back(10)` on a `vector<vector<int>>` quietly creates a 10-element vector.

cards.prompt: What are the modern C++ building blocks for threads and locking?
cards.answer: `std::jthread` (joins automatically on destruction and supports stop tokens), `std::mutex` locked through RAII guards — `std::lock_guard`, `std::unique_lock`, and `std::scoped_lock` for several mutexes at once without deadlock — plus `std::condition_variable` and `std::atomic<T>`.
cards.explanation: Never call `lock()`/`unlock()` by hand: an exception between them leaves the mutex locked forever. A plain `std::thread` that is destroyed while still joinable calls `std::terminate`, which is why `jthread` exists. Data races on non-atomic variables are undefined behaviour.

cards.prompt: What are translation units, header guards and the One Definition Rule?
cards.answer: Each `.cpp` file plus everything it `#include`s is preprocessed into a translation unit and compiled separately; the linker then combines the object files. Header guards or `#pragma once` stop a header being included twice in one TU. The ODR says an entity must have exactly one definition across the program.
cards.explanation: Defining a non-inline function or variable in a header breaks the ODR once two TUs include it (duplicate symbol link errors) — mark it `inline`, or declare in the header and define in one `.cpp`. Every include costs compile time; C++20 modules replace textual inclusion.

cards.prompt: What does "modern CMake" mean?
cards.answer: Target-based configuration: define targets with `add_library`/`add_executable`, attach settings with `target_include_directories`, `target_compile_features` and `target_link_libraries` using PUBLIC/PRIVATE/INTERFACE, and never touch global variables like `CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS`.
cards.explanation: PUBLIC/PRIVATE/INTERFACE control what propagates to dependants, so linking a library brings its include paths and flags automatically. Use a package manager (vcpkg, Conan) or `FetchContent` for dependencies, and presets (`CMakePresets.json`) to share configurations.

cards.prompt: How should a modern C++ codebase handle errors?
cards.answer: Use exceptions for exceptional failures that cannot be handled locally, RAII so unwinding releases everything, and `std::expected`/`std::optional` for expected, frequent failures. Mark functions that cannot throw `noexcept`, and never let an exception escape a destructor.
cards.explanation: Know the exception-safety guarantees: basic (no leaks, valid state), strong (commit-or-rollback), and nothrow. Codebases that ban exceptions (games, some embedded) must use error codes consistently — mixing both styles is the worst of both.
